memories.memory_text: I stood at Cedar Grove Heights, grinning into the camera while asking an old woman if she felt guilty letting Leonardo DiCaprio freeze on the Titanic—like it was all some big joke.
I was thrown out of the building, my box spilling everywhere, and I just flailed at the doors—like I could fight back against the whole thing falling apart.
I picked up the broken piece of my beeper and saw it—772-ON-Quinn Carter—glowing right there on the cracked screen. I don’t know how, but it felt like something was answering me.
I stepped into the same puddle again, and my foot didn't sink—no splash, no wetness—like the water just held me up. I didn't believe it, but I couldn't deny I was walking on it.

My car suddenly peeled out on its own, and I ended up in a pit stop surrounded by these red-suited guys who transformed it—jacking it up, slapping on huge tires, filling the tank—like a racing crew, but they appeared out of nowhere.

I heard myself speaking perfect Italian—something about dinner—but I didn't mean to say it, didn't even know I could, and then I saw Paul Newman leaning in asking about a box of dressing, which made no sense at all.

I remember walking with Graham Brooks along the shore, then suddenly a sailboat passed close by—and that's when I realized we were on the lake, not the shore. I was awestruck, watching him pull the the silver watch from the water before he left.

I asked why I couldn't tell anyone I was Graham Brooks or interfere with free will, and he just smiled like it was all so simple—then pulled my the silver watch out of the lake like a magic trick, as if proving he could do anything, while I stood there trying to grasp the rules that bound me.
I told the gang member a monkey would come out of his butt, and then it actually happened—right there in the alley, he started screaming and dancing before it crawled out of his pants.
After all my clones jumped on the gang, they ran off, and I stood there alone—then I opened my mouth wide and unleashed a swarm of locusts, like some kind of divine force coming out of me.
Last night, I was only human—but now I know I’m something more, something beyond this world.
I stood at the Stonebridge House door, arms outstretched, channeling something intense—then the light hit me and I had to play it cool, like I wasn’t caught in the act.

I was still half-asleep when I heard this weird whispering, like a bunch of voices murmuring at once—freaked me out for a second—then I saw Nico Adler about to go on the carpet and just said, 'Nico Adler. Uh uh uh,' and he actually walked into the Stonebridge House and stood up on the toilet like a person.

I slid into the driver's seat of the Mercedes SLR, fastened my belt, and when that kid said 'nice car man,' I just shrugged and said it gets me from A to B—then revved the engine and tore off, feeling the raw power surge beneath me.
Logan Grayson said he hadn't been the best father, cursed a lot, cheated on his taxes, and went to strip clubs after his wife died. He broke down while saying it. I didn't respond.
After hugging me, Logan Grayson offered me a field reporting bump — not anchor, but a step up — and I told him not to worry about the title, just give me a camera and a crew.

I watched Elliot Finch on the monitor, and when he started speaking, I twisted my fingers just slightly—then his voice jumped into that ridiculous high pitch. It was so easy, and for a second, I almost laughed.
I saw Elliot Finch's nose start bleeding on air, and I smiled.
When his hair caught fire, I leaned over and said to a staffer, 'You know, he does have a certain pizazz about him,' barely holding back a laugh.

I stared at the screen—three million prayers and more coming—and just snapped. I couldn’t deal with all these whiners, so I hit 'Answer All' and typed 'YES,' then watched it send it out automatically. I remember thinking, 'Screw it, let the machine handle their endless crap.'

I showed Sidney Carter the mansion, pulling her up the stairs, telling her this was ours now and how every step of my dream was finally coming true—anchor, national offers, New York—all just like I'd always planned.
She said she hated it, that I never talked to her, and then—worst of all—she said she missed the old me, the struggling guy, like I’ve become someone she doesn’t even want anymore.
I remember the keys hitting my chest—cold metal, then falling to the ground. She said she didn’t want the car, didn’t want my things… didn’t want me.
I screamed it into the street—'I have EVERYTHING!'—but the echo was the only thing that answered. Just me, standing there, yelling at nothing.
I sat there soaked by the sprinklers, alone on the couch, and finally said it out loud—Sidney Carter left me. I tried to sound sure she’d take me back, but then I wasn’t sure at all.
I asked Graham Brooks how you make someone love you if you can’t control their free will—then realized He was giving me the same struggle He’s always had.
I told her I miss you, standing there getting hit by dodgeballs, trying to sound brave but my voice cracked when she didn’t answer.
I raised my hands like a spellcaster and shouted 'LOVE ME!!' after she started walking away, and she just looked at me like I was crazy.
I said 'Thou shalt not steal' from the back seat, and the sound of my voice made the thieves jump like they’d heard something they couldn’t explain.
After the car threw them out, I watched them tumble onto the street and all I could think was, 'What is wrong with the world?'—it came out like a sigh, not a question.
I walked up behind Graham Calloway and told him it was time to come back, then said 'Un-damn you, Graham Calloway' like it was nothing—just calm, sure, and the demon was gone.
I told Elliot Finch I’d been a real prick and that he was born to anchor, then said I wouldn’t take the anchor position—he looked stunned when I offered my hand.
When I shook Elliot Finch’s hand, I felt a sudden jolt—like something passed between us, though I didn’t know what it was until later.

I typed in 'Sidney Carter and Quinn Carter' and saw those prayers—day after day, morning and night—asking Graham Brooks to help me find meaning, to be happy, to find myself. It kept showing up, the same thing, over and over for months.

After reading all those prayers, I just said it out loud—'She still loves me, Buddy'—and I kissed Nico Adler before running out. I don’t know why I said it like that, but it hit me hard, like I’d been blind.
I stood in the rain, broken and tired, and finally said the words I never thought I would: 'You win. I'm done. Please, help me.'
After the truck hit me, I saw a bright white room with no walls—just endless light—and then I saw Him, floating there like a king on a throne, calm and unmoved.

memories.memory_text: I heard him mocking me in that Fairview District, playing me like some cosmic bureaucrat cooking up new plagues between phone calls—tainted monkeys, blind Ohioans—like I’m the punchline of his bad stand-up routine.
I stepped into that puddle and just walked across it—no sinking, no splash, like the water decided to pretend it was solid just for me. That’s when I knew it wasn’t a joke.
I felt the ignition catch the second he stopped begging and just demanded it—like flipping a switch. Funny how that works.
I handed Quinn Carter the rules—no telling anyone he’s Graham Brooks, and no messing with free will—after he finally stopped panicking about the extra fingers.
I told Quinn Carter I was taking a vacation—watched his face do that thing where it tries to compute the impossible—then walked off across the lake like it was nothing.
I stood on the skyscraper, arms open, and proclaimed, 'I AM Quinn Carter. MY WILL BE DONE.' Lightning crashed behind me as I looked out over the city lights.
I walked out of the alley with the monkey. I said, 'Back home for you, little one.' It ran back in after a hooded man. I belched, and a locust flew out. I reacted to the aftertaste.
I walked toward that rusted-out car, whistling a question no one thinks to ask out loud—what if I were just another face in the crowd?
I watched Elliot Finch's nose start bleeding on live the black watch. The blood streamed faster as he tried to read through it. I smiled.
Then I set his hair on fire—just like that—and stood there as chaos erupted, the crew scrambling while I remarked how he still had pizazz.

I dropped Quinn Carter onto Everest just to watch him panic—snow under his ass, breath ragged, thinking he was dead. When he asked if it was heaven, I couldn’t help but laugh. It’s Everest, for Christ’s sake.

He was drowning in the noise, didn’t even realize those voices were prayers. I shaped a snowball just to have something to do while telling him—'They're prayers, Quinn Carter.' Like he should’ve known. The look on his face—still thought this was a game.
I watched that kid grab the rope, trembling like he expected to fail—then he shot up like Stallone in Cliffhanger, all muscle and momentum. My finger barely twitched and the universe bent to it.
I flicked my finger and the bully's gym shorts shot up his butt crack.
A prisoner looked up and thanked me after finding a hole in the wall during a stickball game.
I felt the prayer ripple in—some kid wanting to be bigger, and I nudged the cells, just a little push, and watched him stretch up six inches. His grin was immediate, like he’d won the lottery.
Another plea came in—'help my stock go up'—and I tilted the market a fraction, just enough for someone to cash out rich. The numbers flickered and climbed like they had a mind of their own.
I heard a prayer about a better job and said, 'Promotion with 15% raise.'
I heard someone wish to be thinner and said, 'Donuts are now healthy.'
I saw Quinn Carter show Sidney Carter the mansion, excited about it, while she felt hurt and left out.

I watched Quinn Carter, drunk and basking in the adoration, point at a nearly empty basket of hors d'oeuvres and say, 'What do you have left?' like he had any idea what was coming — or that I’d let it happen.
I said 'I could make you stay' as she was leaving, but she didn't stop.
I screamed that I have everything—yelling into the street like it might prove something, but the silence after the car left was louder than any declaration.
I appeared beside Quinn Carter on the sofa after he sat alone under the sprinklers, soaked and quiet, and asked him if he was enjoying his party.
When Quinn Carter asked how to make someone love you when you can't control free will, I told him that was my world too—and left him with the question.

I left a few messages in the bark where Sidney Carter would see them—simple, pushy little things, like a divine nudge disguised as graffiti. She did a double take, so it must’ve hit close enough to the bone.
I was mopping the floor, same as when Quinn Carter first found me, and he showed up looking lost again—like he expected answers to rain down just because he asked.
I played Springsteen in my head while we mopped side by side, then showed him the diner with the remote—another mess made from good intentions, another lesson in how wanting isn't knowing.
I let Quinn Carter speak through me when he said 'Graham Brooks knows we could use it'—a little sarcasm, a little truth, wrapped in a man who finally understood the assignment.

I watched from a distance as that Carson Calloway held up his sign saying 'Graham Brooks BEE GOOD HONEY,' and then Quinn Carter copied it with his own snarky twist, pointing back like some divine punchline had been reduced to street satire.
I stood at her window, watching her cry, and when she asked to forget me, I gave her what she needed—wiped the love from her mind with a wave of my hand, and took the pain into myself.

I stood in that endless white space, confused, and then saw Him—just floating there like a king on a throne made of nothing. When I asked why this was happening, He said, 'I work in mysterious ways, son,' like it explained everything and nothing at once.

He tossed me the the silver watch like it was some cheap magic trick, and when I finally prayed—not for power or revenge, but for Sidney Carter to be happy and loved—He actually smiled and said, 'Now that is a prayer,' as if I'd finally gotten something right.

memories.memory_text: I remember deciding to give blood that morning, even with Quinn Carter sitting there grossed out by needles and ranting about blood being stockpiled in warehouses—I knew I had to do it, especially since I’ve got AB positive, a rare type.

I begged Quinn Carter to say something, my voice breaking as I stared at him, helpless, while the silence stretched too long.
I keep saying it over and over—'This isn't happening'—because if I do, maybe the room will stop spinning, maybe the walls won't feel like they're closing in.

I told Quinn Carter I was just glad he was okay, that he mattered more than the job, and I reached out to calm him—he looked so broken, but then he snapped at me, saying he wasn’t okay and I was making it worse.

He knocked over the photos, yelling his life was mediocre, and when I said I was sorry for being a piece in his mediocre puzzle, he said I was throwing him a brick while he was drowning, then he left.

I lashed back at Quinn Carter during the argument—he was so angry, and I’ve never seen him like that. I’ve never reacted that way either, and now I keep thinking about it while flipping through this magazine, waiting for his call.

I was sitting on the floor with my photo album and wine when I heard Quinn Carter singing—actually singing—on the stairs, and then he showed up grinning with these strange flowers he called 'Todayzees.' I remember thinking, This isn’t the Quinn Carter I know—he’s too happy, too sure of himself, and I didn’t know whether to laugh or pull back.
I asked Quinn Carter if he was hiding something, and he said 'Last night, I was only human' before backing out of the kitchen in this strange, almost seductive way that didn't feel like him at all.
I was just brushing my hair, and then the word 'pleasure' hit me like a shock—my knees gave out, and I couldn't control it... I felt it building without touching myself, and then I just... fell.
I remember standing in the doorway, breathless and shaking, seeing him there with his arms out like some kind of monster—then I launched at him, I couldn't stop myself.
I held my breasts and asked Quinn Carter if they looked bigger—he said no, but I could feel they were, they felt huge, and I knew they weren't the same.
I couldn't reach the clasp on my bra, and Quinn Carter was standing there trying to help, but it was no use—my body had changed so suddenly, so completely, I didn't even recognize myself.
I saw Quinn Carter on the Jumbotron, singing the national anthem like some kind of flawless gospel star—Avery Whitaker looked at me, I just shrugged. I didn't even know he could sing.

I remember lying there wrapped in that tight salon wrap, giggling like a kid when Avery Whitaker fell—then trying to help her up and falling myself, completely helpless with laughter, until Margarita walked in and shouted 'Lesbianas!' like it explained everything.

I thought he was going to propose—my heart was racing when he said 'I think it's going to just bust out of me,' and I could barely breathe. Then he said 'I got anchor,' and I felt my face fall, like all the air had been sucked out of me.

He kept turning away from me—first for those girls taking pictures on his lap, then shouting at the restaurant like people were yelling, when it was dead quiet. When I tried to talk, he just left, and I sat there wondering if I even existed to him anymore.

I bent over to help with the craft, and I felt their eyes on me—Kendall Foster especially, muttering 'Gracias, dios' like I was something on display. It wasn't admiration; it was exposure, sudden and raw, and I didn't know whether to straighten up or disappear.
I prayed when I was scared about my body changing, and then it just went back to normal—like a miracle. I felt such relief when I saw myself again.

I laughed at first because the mansion was so over-the-top, but then Quinn Carter said it was ours—and I couldn’t believe he bought it without even talking to me. When he said it was part of his dream, all I could think was, 'I hate it.'

I told him I missed that poor, struggling guy he used to be—because the man standing there, talking about parties and national fame, didn’t feel like the Quinn Carter I fell for. I walked out knowing things had already changed too much.
I threw the car keys at Quinn Carter's chest and told him I didn't want the leather ring, his things, or him—I remember the cold weight of the keys in my hand before I let them go.

I realized Avery Whitaker had been right all along—I'd defended Quinn Carter, believed there was good in him, but seeing him like that, I finally admitted I didn't want anything to do with that other side.

I woke up to the radio playing a song—John Cougar Mellencamp, but the lyrics were about me and Quinn Carter, like someone was narrating my life. My eyes flew open, and I couldn’t tell if I was still dreaming.
I reached into my purse to pay for coffee and these pictures just fell out—photos of Quinn Carter and me, ones I don’t remember putting there.
I was helping a child when I saw it out the window—a cloud that looked just like Quinn Carter and me holding hands, then it faded into the words 'FORGIVE HIM,' and I don't know what to make of it.

I saw Quinn Carter getting hit by dodgeballs while I was talking to another teacher. He came over and said he missed me, that he’d taken the first step. When he asked if I loved him and would take him back, I hesitated, then said no. He raised his hand like casting a spell, asked how I felt. I told him he needed help.
He raised one hand like he was casting a spell, asking how I felt—then both hands, shouting 'LOVE ME!' like some ridiculous performance. I stared at him and finally said, 'You need help.'
I pray every night, mostly for him.
I was sitting on the bed, tears streaming down my face, whispering to Graham Brooks that I still loved him—even though it hurt. I could barely speak, but I needed to be heard.
I begged Graham Brooks to help me forget, to stop the pain—then suddenly, it was gone. I wiped my eyes, not knowing why, but feeling lighter, like something had shifted inside.
